items.title: Level 2: Why the Civil Service uses Success Profiles
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Before Success Profiles, the Civil Service chose staff mainly by asking for examples of competencies. Success Profiles was introduced to give a wider and fairer picture of a candidate. The idea is that every job is described using the same five elements: Behaviours, Strengths, Ability, Experience and Technical. A recruiting manager looks at the job and decides which of the five matter most. Some jobs lean on Ability and Behaviours. Others also ask for Technical skills. The advert then says which will be assessed and how, for example through a form, a test, or an interview. Because the framework is flexible, it lets the Civil Service look at more than a person's job history. A candidate with little paid work can still show Behaviours, Strengths and Ability. This helps to open the Civil Service to people from many backgrounds. It also helps to make selection fairer, because all candidates for a job are judged against the same list of requirements. For you as an applicant, the main lesson is to read each advert carefully. It tells you what is being looked for, so you can match your evidence to it instead of guessing. The framework applies at every grade, from Administrative Officer to the Senior Civil Service, though the level of what is expected changes as the grade goes up.

questions.prompt: Why was Success Profiles introduced?

options.text: To replace all job interviews with short online tests
To reduce the number of people who are able to apply
To make every job in government use identical requirements
To give a wider and fairer picture of each candidate

questions.hint: It was designed to look at more than job history, so selection is wider and fairer.

questions.prompt: How does a recruiting manager use the five elements?

options.text: Choosing which of them matter most for the job
Using only the first two on the list for every vacancy
Letting each candidate pick the ones they prefer to show
Applying all five equally to every post in the department

questions.hint: Managers decide which elements fit the job, and the advert says which.

questions.prompt: What does the advert tell you about the elements?

options.text: How many people have applied so far
What the final scores must be
Which will be assessed, and how
Which candidates did best last time

questions.hint: The advert states which elements are assessed and the methods used.

questions.prompt: Why does the flexible design help people with little paid work?

options.text: Experience is never assessed for entry-level roles at all
Several elements can be shown without a long job history
Paid work is not accepted as evidence in most adverts
Technical skills replace all of the other four elements

questions.hint: Several elements can be shown without much paid work.

questions.prompt: Why is selection fairer when all candidates are judged on the same list?

options.text: Everyone has the same interview questions word for word
Nobody sees the requirements beforehand
Everyone is compared with the same requirements
Everyone receives the same score by default

questions.hint: A shared list of requirements gives a level basis for comparison.

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson for an applicant about reading adverts?

options.text: Match your evidence to what the advert asks for
Apply the same set of answers to every job you see
Ignore the listed items and use your own headings instead
Write one long general account of your whole life story

questions.hint: Matching evidence to the stated requirements is the main tip.

questions.prompt: Which pair of methods might an advert use to assess elements?

options.text: A form, a test or an interview
A reference or a medical
A trial shift or a swimming test
A phone call or a postcard

questions.hint: Adverts commonly use application forms, online tests and interviews.

questions.prompt: At which grades does Success Profiles apply?

options.text: Every grade, from Administrative Officer upwards
Only jobs that need a degree
Only the most senior grades
Only Administrative Officer and Assistant grades

questions.hint: It applies across all grades, with expectations rising as grade rises.

questions.prompt: What changes as the grade of the job goes up?

options.text: The number of elements, which always rises to nine
The level of what is expected
The need for an advert
The use of Success Profiles, which stops at senior grades

questions.hint: The framework stays, but the level of expectation increases.

questions.prompt: What did the Civil Service rely on mainly before Success Profiles?

options.text: Personality profiles
Competency examples
Written exams only
Employer references only

questions.hint: Before Success Profiles, selection focused mainly on competencies.

items.title: Level 2: Reading a Civil Service job advert
items.body: A job advert on Civil Service Jobs is the best guide to what you must prove. Most adverts begin with a summary of the role, the grade, the salary range, the location and the closing date. Lower down there is a section on the person specification and how candidates will be assessed. This is where the Success Profiles elements are listed. For an entry-level Administrative Officer role you might see a few Behaviours, for example Communicating and Influencing, Working Together and Delivering at Pace, with the note that they will be tested at a lower level. You may also see a Strengths or Ability element, and sometimes a short Experience requirement. The advert will say how each is checked. Some are assessed on the application form, some by online tests, and some at interview. The advert may also mention the number of stages and the dates, and how to ask for a reasonable adjustment if you need one. The sensible way to read an advert is to underline each element and Behaviour, then write one or two examples against each. If a Behaviour is not listed, you do not need an example for it. If a requirement is listed as essential, make sure you cover it. Keep the advert, because the details can change after the closing date.

questions.prompt: Which part of an advert lists the Success Profiles elements?

options.text: The summary of the salary, grade and job location
The notice showing the closing date for applications
The list of other related vacancies in the department
The person specification and assessment section

questions.hint: The assessment section is where the elements and Behaviours appear.

questions.prompt: What does the summary at the start of an advert usually show?

options.text: The names and job titles of everyone on the interview panel
The role, grade, salary range, location and closing date
The full list of questions to be asked at the interview
The scores gained by earlier candidates for the same post

questions.hint: The summary gives basic facts about the job and deadline.

questions.prompt: What might an entry-level advert say about the Behaviours it lists?

options.text: They will be tested at every level
They are optional to answer
They will be tested at a lower level
They will be tested only on the form

questions.hint: Entry roles use the lower levels of the Behaviours.

questions.prompt: How may different elements be checked in one recruitment?

options.text: All of them on the application form alone
All of them by one long online test at the start
All of them at a single interview on one day
Some on the form, some by tests, some at interview

questions.hint: Different stages can test different elements.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible first step with an advert?

options.text: Copy the answers given by another applicant who got in
Underline each element and Behaviour it lists
Write one long answer meant to cover everything it mentions
Wait until the interview before you start preparing

questions.hint: Highlighting the requirements helps you plan your evidence.

questions.prompt: If a Behaviour is not listed in the advert, what do you need?

options.text: An example for it anyway, to be safe
Nothing extra for it, as only listed ones count
A reference who can speak about it
A short test taken before the interview

questions.hint: You only need evidence for the Behaviours the advert lists.

questions.prompt: Why should you keep a copy of the advert?

options.text: It can be used in place of the application form
It acts as proof that you are eligible to apply
The details can change after the closing date
You must hand the copy back to the panel at interview

questions.hint: Keeping a copy lets you check the original requirements later.

questions.prompt: What may an advert tell you about adjustments?

options.text: How to be excused from taking any online test
How your score will be changed if you receive one
How to ask for a reasonable adjustment
Which kinds of candidate are expected to need one

questions.hint: Adverts explain how to request support if you need it.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviours might an entry-level advert name?

options.text: Every one of the nine Behaviours without exception
Leadership, Seeing the Big Picture and Managing a Quality Service for all roles
Changing and Improving for every role
Communicating and Influencing, Working Together and Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: Entry-level adverts often name a few of the nine, such as those listed.

questions.prompt: What does an essential requirement mean for your application?

options.text: You can skip it if short of space
It applies to other candidates
You must make sure you cover it
It is only a suggestion

questions.hint: Essential requirements must be addressed in your application.

items.title: Level 2: Seeing the Big Picture and Changing and Improving explained
items.body: Seeing the Big Picture and Changing and Improving are linked, but they are not the same. Seeing the Big Picture is about understanding. At entry level, it means knowing how your job supports your team, your department and the public. If you process a claim, you know that a real person is waiting for the result. If you file a record, you know that someone later must be able to find it. The wider picture also includes being aware of what is happening around your work, such as new rules or changes to a service. Changing and Improving is about action. It means being open to new ideas, suggesting better ways, and helping new systems to work. At entry level, you are not expected to redesign a service. You are expected to notice what could work better and to say so politely, and to give a change a fair try rather than resist it. A person can show both together. For example, someone who understands that late letters upset customers might suggest a reminder system and then help to set it up. In an application you would explain the problem you saw, what you suggested or did, and what improved as a result. Small and real examples are better than large and made-up ones.

questions.prompt: What is Seeing the Big Picture mainly about?

options.text: Working extra hours whenever a task is behind schedule
Making changes to systems that you personally dislike
Deciding which person should lead each project in the team
Understanding how your job supports the team and the public

questions.hint: It is about understanding the purpose and wider context of your work.

questions.prompt: What is Changing and Improving mainly about?

options.text: Coaching a colleague who has recently joined the team
Being open to new ideas and suggesting better ways
Knowing why your own job exists in the department
Meeting every deadline in a busy and difficult week

questions.hint: It is about taking action to improve things and accepting change.

questions.prompt: Why does an entry-level processor of claims need to see the big picture?

options.text: The processor reports directly to ministers
A real person is waiting for the result
The processor is the one who sets the policy
The processor chooses which rules are applied

questions.hint: It reminds the worker that each claim affects a real person.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign of Changing and Improving at entry level?

options.text: Keeping to the old method because it feels familiar
Redesigning a whole service on your own initiative
Giving a new system a fair try instead of resisting it
Waiting for management to find every problem for you

questions.hint: Accepting and testing change is part of this Behaviour.

questions.prompt: How is Changing and Improving different from Seeing the Big Picture?

options.text: It is used only at senior levels, while the other is not
It is only asked of managers, while the other is for all
It is about action, while the other is about understanding
It is about deadlines, while the other is about accuracy

questions.hint: One is understanding the context, the other is acting to improve things.

questions.prompt: Someone suggests a reminder system for late letters and helps set it up. What does this mainly show?

options.text: Changing and Improving
Delivering at Pace
Managing a Quality Service
Leadership

questions.hint: Suggesting and helping to carry out an improvement shows Changing and Improving.

questions.prompt: Knowing that a record you file must be found later most clearly shows what?

options.text: Delivering at Pace
Seeing the Big Picture
Developing Self and Others
Communicating and Influencing

questions.hint: Understanding the later use of your work shows Seeing the Big Picture.

questions.prompt: What should an entry-level person do on noticing a task that could be simpler?

options.text: Ignore it because it is not part of their own job
Say so politely to a manager or colleague
Change it quietly overnight without telling anyone
Wait until promoted before speaking up about it

questions.hint: Politely raising the idea is expected at this level.

questions.prompt: What should an application example for Changing and Improving contain?

options.text: A list of ideas you might have in the future
A description of what your own manager's role involves
A general opinion on whether change is a good thing
The problem, what you did and what improved

questions.hint: Say what was wrong, what you did and the effect.

questions.prompt: Which type of example is better for these Behaviours?

options.text: Short and secondhand
Long and general
Large and made-up
Small and real

questions.hint: Small, real examples are better than big, invented ones.

items.title: Level 2: Making Effective Decisions and Leadership explained
items.body: Making Effective Decisions is about reaching a sensible choice using the right information. At entry level, this does not mean taking big risks. It means finding out the facts, thinking about the options, asking for advice when you are unsure, and following the rules that apply. It also means being able to explain why you chose as you did. For example, when a customer asks for something unusual, a good decision-maker checks the guidance, asks a more senior colleague if still unsure, and records what was decided. Leadership at entry level is different from managing people. It is about being positive, treating everyone with respect, and setting a good example. It includes helping a new colleague settle in, staying calm when the work is busy, and speaking up politely when something seems wrong. A leader at this level also takes responsibility for mistakes and learns from them. The two Behaviours can overlap, because making a fair decision in front of others can show leadership. The difference is the focus: decisions are about choosing, while Leadership is about the way you behave and influence the mood around you. In an application, avoid saying you are a natural leader. Describe what you did, and the effect on others.

questions.prompt: What is Making Effective Decisions mainly about?

options.text: Reaching a sensible choice using the right information
Taking big risks quickly whenever time is short
Leaving every choice to the people more senior than you
Always picking the cheapest option on the table

questions.hint: It means weighing facts and options to reach a sound choice.

questions.prompt: What should a good decision-maker do when a customer asks for something unusual?

options.text: Agree straight away so that the customer stays happy
Check the guidance and ask a senior colleague if unsure
Pass the request along without keeping any record of it
Refuse at once without checking whether it is allowed

questions.hint: Checking guidance and asking for advice are part of a sound decision.

questions.prompt: Why record what was decided?

options.text: So that the customer does not have to be told of it
So the choice can be explained later on
So that nobody else in the team is able to see it
So that the same request is never considered again

questions.hint: Being able to explain a decision is part of making it effectively.

questions.prompt: How does entry-level Leadership differ from managing people?

options.text: It applies only at senior grades and not at entry level
It means giving orders that others must follow
It is about attitude and example, not having staff
It requires leading a team of at least ten people

questions.hint: Entry-level Leadership is shown through behaviour and example.

questions.prompt: Which of these shows Leadership at entry level?

options.text: Helping a new colleague settle in
Blaming others for errors
Keeping to yourself when busy
Taking over a task without asking

questions.hint: Supporting others is a typical entry-level example.

questions.prompt: What does a leader at this level do when they make a mistake?

options.text: Wait for someone else to find it and put it right
Say that the whole team shared the error equally
Hide it for as long as it takes to be noticed
Take responsibility for it and learn from it

questions.hint: Owning mistakes is part of showing Leadership.

questions.prompt: How do decisions and Leadership differ in focus?

options.text: Decisions are made in writing, Leadership is spoken only
Decisions are for managers only, Leadership is for all
Decisions are about choosing, Leadership is about conduct
Decisions are about people, Leadership is about money

questions.hint: One is about the choice, the other is about conduct and influence.

questions.prompt: What should you avoid saying in an application about Leadership?

options.text: That you are a natural leader, with nothing to back it up
What you did and what effect it had on others
How a colleague responded to what you did
A real example taken from your home or community life

questions.hint: Claims without evidence are weak; describe actions instead.

questions.prompt: Staying calm and helping others in a busy week mainly shows which Behaviour?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Making Effective Decisions
Changing and Improving
Leadership

questions.hint: Calm and supportive behaviour under pressure shows Leadership.

questions.prompt: Comparing two options and asking for advice before picking one mainly shows which Behaviour?

options.text: Delivering at Pace under pressure
Working Together with other people
Making Effective Decisions
Leadership and setting an example

questions.hint: Weighing options and seeking advice shows decision-making.

items.title: Level 2: Communicating and Influencing compared with Working Together
items.body: Communicating and Influencing and Working Together often appear in the same advert, and people sometimes mix them up. Communicating and Influencing is about the message. At entry level it means speaking and writing clearly, listening carefully, adapting how you speak to the person in front of you, and explaining your reasons politely when you want others to agree. It also covers using plain language and checking that people have understood. Working Together is about the relationships. It means supporting colleagues, sharing information, treating people with respect, valuing different views and backgrounds, and doing your fair share of the work so that the team succeeds. A helpful way to tell them apart is to ask what the example is mainly about. If it is about getting a message across, such as a clear letter, a telephone call with an upset customer or a short presentation, it is Communicating and Influencing. If it is about cooperating, such as covering for a colleague or solving a problem with others, it is Working Together. Many real examples show both, and you may be asked for one example for each. In that case choose different situations so the assessor sees two distinct pieces of evidence. Always say what you did and what happened.

questions.prompt: Communicating and Influencing is mainly about what?

options.text: The message and how you share it
The quality of the customer records you keep
The relationships between members of a team
The speed at which you finish each piece of work

questions.hint: It covers speaking, writing, listening and explaining your reasons.

questions.prompt: Working Together is mainly about what?

options.text: Writing clear and well-organised letters to customers
Reaching decisions on your own without delay
Cooperating with others and doing your share
Meeting the individual targets you have been set

questions.hint: It is about collaboration and supporting colleagues.

questions.prompt: Which is part of Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Learning something useful from a mistake you made
Covering a colleague's shift when they are away
Adapting how you speak to the person in front of you
Keeping the shared drive tidy and well organised

questions.hint: Adapting your style to the audience is a communication skill.

questions.prompt: Which is part of Working Together?

options.text: Writing a letter in plain English for a customer
Doing your fair share so the team succeeds
Checking that a listener has fully understood you
Explaining your reasons politely to someone who disagrees

questions.hint: Fair contribution to the team is a Working Together action.

questions.prompt: A call with an upset customer is mainly which Behaviour?

options.text: Communicating and Influencing
Managing a Quality Service for the department
Changing and Improving a procedure
Working Together and sharing out tasks

questions.hint: Handling a conversation clearly and calmly is communication.

questions.prompt: Covering for a colleague so a job is finished mainly shows which Behaviour?

options.text: Working Together
Communicating and Influencing
Delivering at Pace
Making Effective Decisions

questions.hint: Supporting a colleague is cooperation.

questions.prompt: How can you tell the two Behaviours apart in an example?

options.text: See whether the example happened in a paid workplace
Check the name of the manager involved in the story
Look at how many lines the whole example takes up
Ask whether it is mainly about the message or cooperating

questions.hint: The focus of the example tells you which Behaviour it shows.

questions.prompt: If an advert asks for both, what is the best approach?

options.text: Skip one of the two
Write one example without a result
Use the same example twice word for word
Choose different situations for each

questions.hint: Two distinct examples give the assessor two pieces of evidence.

questions.prompt: What does using plain language involve?

options.text: Using exactly the same wording for every reader
Choosing simple words the reader will understand
Using technical terms so you sound like an expert
Writing as briefly as you possibly can in every case

questions.hint: Plain language is clear and suited to the reader.

questions.prompt: Valuing different views and backgrounds is most closely linked to which Behaviour?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Managing a Quality Service
Delivering at Pace
Working Together

questions.hint: Respecting difference is part of working well with others.

items.title: Level 2: Learning, quality and pace explained
items.body: Three Behaviours describe a reliable worker. Developing Self and Others is about learning. At entry level you take responsibility for your own development, ask for feedback and use it, learn from mistakes, and help colleagues who are newer than you. It might be going on a course, learning a new system or showing someone how to do a task. Managing a Quality Service is about doing the work well for the people who rely on it. You follow procedures, check your work, keep accurate records and treat customers politely and fairly. If something goes wrong you put it right and tell someone who needs to know. Delivering at Pace is about getting things done on time. You plan your work, work out what is most urgent, keep going when it is busy and ask for help early if a deadline is at risk. A useful way to separate them is by what you want to show. Accuracy and care point to Managing a Quality Service. Time and priorities point to Delivering at Pace. Growth and sharing knowledge point to Developing Self and Others. Real examples often show more than one, but an application answer should be built around one Behaviour. Give the details: what you learned, what you checked, or what you finished by when.

questions.prompt: Developing Self and Others is mainly about what?

options.text: Planning and keeping to a household budget
Learning and helping others to learn
Giving accurate and polite service to customers
Meeting deadlines in a busy week at work

questions.hint: It covers your own development and supporting other people's.

questions.prompt: Managing a Quality Service is mainly about what?

options.text: Getting every piece of work done as fast as possible
Learning how to use new systems and software
Doing the work well for the people who rely on it
Leading a team of people through a time of change

questions.hint: It concerns accuracy, courtesy and reliability for customers.

questions.prompt: Delivering at Pace is mainly about what?

options.text: Checking every piece of work carefully for errors
Giving regular feedback to others in the team
Suggesting improvements to the way a service runs
Getting work done on time and prioritising well

questions.hint: It concerns planning, priorities and meeting deadlines.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows Developing Self and Others?

options.text: Asking for feedback and using it
Working faster than everybody else in the team
Avoiding any new system until it has been proved
Checking each record a second time before filing

questions.hint: Seeking and using feedback is part of developing yourself.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Suggesting a new layout
Volunteering for training
Keeping accurate records
Rushing to clear a queue

questions.hint: Accurate records support a reliable service.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows Delivering at Pace?

options.text: Rechecking a finished letter until it looks perfect
Sharing a useful skill with a colleague who asks
Asking for help early when a deadline is at risk
Learning a new software package in your own time

questions.hint: Raising a risk early helps meet deadlines.

questions.prompt: What should someone do on finding a mistake in a service they provide?

options.text: Put it right and tell the people who need to know
Wait for a complaint to arrive before doing anything
Pass the job to a colleague without explaining why
Hope that nobody notices it before it is forgotten

questions.hint: Correcting and reporting an error is part of a quality service.

questions.prompt: Accuracy and care in an example point most to which Behaviour?

options.text: Developing Self and Others
Delivering at Pace
Leadership
Managing a Quality Service

questions.hint: Care and accuracy show quality of service.

questions.prompt: Time and priorities in an example point most to which Behaviour?

options.text: Developing Self and Others
Communicating and Influencing
Delivering at Pace
Managing a Quality Service

questions.hint: Planning around time is Delivering at Pace.

questions.prompt: Showing a new colleague how to use a system mainly shows which Behaviour?

options.text: Developing Self and Others
Managing a Quality Service
Delivering at Pace
Making Effective Decisions

questions.hint: Teaching others is part of developing others.

items.title: Level 2: How Strengths differ from Behaviours
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Strengths and Behaviours are both assessed at interview, but they work in different ways. Behaviours look at what you have done. You are asked for a real example from the past, and you answer using the STAR structure. The assessor scores the example against the Behaviour description for the grade. Strengths look at what you naturally do well and enjoy. The questions are often shorter and quicker, and there is no need for a past example. A strengths question might ask whether you prefer to finish a task before moving on or to juggle several at once, or what you enjoy most about helping people. The interviewer listens for energy, enthusiasm and honesty in your answer. Because a strengths answer should be natural, rehearsing a script can work against you. Preparation means knowing yourself. Think about what you are good at, what you look forward to, and what you find draining. Also read the role so that you understand what it involves. Behaviours questions reward preparation with specific, rehearsed examples. Strengths questions reward honest, spontaneous answers. Some interviews mix the two, so make sure you know which sort of question you are being asked. The advert will say whether strengths are tested.

questions.prompt: What do Behaviours questions ask for?

options.text: A comment on the interviewer
A prediction of your future
A statement of what you enjoy
A real example from your past

questions.hint: Behaviours questions ask what you have done before.

questions.prompt: What do strengths questions look at?

options.text: What you naturally do well and enjoy
What you were paid to do in previous jobs
What you have been formally trained to do
What qualifications you have gained so far

questions.hint: Strengths questions explore natural talent and enjoyment.

questions.prompt: How are strengths questions usually put?

options.text: In writing only
With a prepared worksheet
Long and detailed
Short and quick

questions.hint: Strengths questions tend to be brief and fast.

questions.prompt: Which structure should you use to answer a Behaviours question?

options.text: A single sentence
A short story with no ending
A list of words
STAR

questions.hint: STAR is the standard structure for Behaviours answers.

questions.prompt: What does an interviewer listen for in a strengths answer?

options.text: Phrases learned from a book of model answers
Exact figures and dates for everything you mention
Technical words that show professional knowledge
Energy, enthusiasm and honesty in how you answer

questions.hint: Interviewers listen to how you talk about the subject.

questions.prompt: Why might rehearsing a script hurt a strengths answer?

options.text: The answer must be longer
The question changes each time
The panel cannot hear a script
The answer should be natural

questions.hint: Strengths answers should come across as natural.

questions.prompt: How should you prepare for strengths questions?

options.text: Know what you are good at and what you enjoy
Learn a list of model answers from a book or website
Practise answering with STAR for every question
Memorise the wording of the job advert closely

questions.hint: Knowing yourself is the best preparation.

questions.prompt: A question asks whether you prefer to finish one task before starting another. What kind is it?

options.text: A technical question
An ability test item
A strengths question
A Behaviours question

questions.hint: Preference questions are typical of strengths-based interviews.

questions.prompt: Tell us about a time when you helped a colleague. What kind of question is this?

options.text: A Behaviours question
An Ability test item
A Technical question
A strengths question

questions.hint: It asks for a past example, which is a Behaviours question.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when an interview mixes the two types?

options.text: You need to recognise which type each question is
You must change the order in which you give answers
You can use STAR as the answer to everything
You can rely on a rehearsed script for all of it

questions.hint: Each question needs a suitable style of answer.

items.title: Level 2: Ability tests and Technical requirements explained
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Ability and Technical sound alike, but they ask different things. Ability is about your capacity to learn and do tasks. Employers measure it with short online tests under time pressure, such as a verbal reasoning test that checks how well you understand written information, a numerical reasoning test that checks how well you work with figures, and a judgement test that checks how you decide what to do in work situations. You do not need a qualification to take them. They ask for a general aptitude and not knowledge from a course. Practising sample tests helps because you will know the layout and how fast you must work. Technical is about specific skills or qualifications that the job needs before you start. An example is a professional accountancy qualification for a finance role, or a licence needed to do a certain job. Because administrative jobs often involve general office tasks, many do not list a Technical requirement. When one is listed, the advert names it clearly and says whether you must hold it when you apply. If you do not meet an essential Technical requirement, you will probably not be able to progress. If you are unsure whether a requirement applies to you, the contact details on the advert can help. Read the section carefully before you apply.

questions.prompt: What is Ability mainly about?

options.text: How much you enjoy the work you are asked to do
The qualifications you already hold for the work
Your capacity to learn and do tasks
The kinds of job you have had in the past

questions.hint: Ability is aptitude and potential.

questions.prompt: What does a verbal reasoning test check about you?

options.text: How well you understand written information
How well you work with figures and tables
How quickly you can type a passage of text
How well you can remember a list of names

questions.hint: Verbal reasoning is about written information.

questions.prompt: What does a numerical reasoning test check?

options.text: How well you remember names
How well you decide in work situations
How well you work with figures
How well you understand reading passages

questions.hint: Numerical reasoning is about numbers and data.

questions.prompt: What does a judgement test check?

options.text: How accurately you can spell words in a report
How you decide what to do in work situations
How quickly you can read a long passage of text
How much you can remember from a short briefing

questions.hint: Judgement tests present work scenarios and ask what you would do.

questions.prompt: Why does practising sample tests help?

options.text: The real test uses exactly the same questions again
You can find out in advance what the pass mark is
The practice removes the time limit on the real test
You learn the layout and how fast you must work

questions.hint: Familiarity with format and pace improves performance.

questions.prompt: What is Technical mainly about?

options.text: Any volunteering work you have done in the past
Whether you enjoy the kind of work in the role
A general ability to learn new tasks quickly
Specific skills or qualifications needed before starting

questions.hint: Technical covers named skills or qualifications for the job.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of a Technical requirement?

options.text: Enjoyment of helping members of the public
A professional accountancy qualification
The ability to pick up new tasks quickly
Being punctual and reliable at all times

questions.hint: An accountancy qualification is a named professional requirement.

questions.prompt: Why do many administrative jobs list no Technical requirement?

options.text: They involve general office tasks
They are filled using Ability tests as the only measure
They are thought never to need any skills at all
They are not treated as proper jobs by the department

questions.hint: General office roles seldom need professional qualifications.

questions.prompt: What does the advert say about a listed Technical requirement?

options.text: Only the starting salary for those who meet it
What it is and whether you must hold it when you apply
Only the grade of the person who would assess it
Only the date by which you must have gained it

questions.hint: Adverts name the requirement and the timing.

questions.prompt: Whom can you contact if unsure whether a requirement applies?

options.text: The contact named on the advert
Another applicant for the same vacancy
A friend who works in a different department
Your most recent employer or manager

questions.hint: The advert gives contact details for questions.

items.title: Level 2: Where evidence for Behaviours can come from
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Many applicants think they need a long work history to prove the Behaviours. This is not so. A good example can come from many parts of life. At work, it might be a busy shift in a shop, a project at a previous employer or a day on a work placement. At home, it might be organising care for a relative, running the household budget or managing family appointments. In the community, it might be volunteering, helping at a school, coaching a sports team or serving on a committee. In education, it might be a group assignment, a course or a college event. What matters is that you can describe what you did and show the Behaviour in action. For example, helping to run a stall at a school fair can show Working Together, while explaining a form to a neighbour can show Communicating and Influencing. A good strategy is to make a list of six to eight things you are proud of, then match each to one or two Behaviours. This is easier than starting from the Behaviours and trying to find an example. Keep the examples recent if you can, but older ones are fine if they are strong. Always make sure that an example is true and that you can answer follow-up questions about it.

questions.prompt: How much work history do you need in order to prove the Behaviours?

options.text: Civil Service jobs only, with a start date
At least five years in a paid job
Examples can come from many parts of life
Paid jobs only, with a reference from each

questions.hint: Evidence can come from work, home, community and education.

questions.prompt: Which of these could provide evidence for a Behaviour?

options.text: Organising care for a relative
Following a popular series on television
Reading a daily newspaper from cover to cover
Watching a training video through to the end

questions.hint: Organising care is an activity involving real skills.

questions.prompt: Which example might show Working Together?

options.text: Helping to run a stall at a school fair
Filling in your own tax return on time
Reading a book in the evening to relax
Training alone for a long-distance run

questions.hint: Cooperating with others at an event shows teamwork.

questions.prompt: Which example might show Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Explaining a form to a neighbour
Cooking a family meal from fresh ingredients
Painting the fence around your garden
Carrying out the weekly shopping on your own

questions.hint: Explaining something clearly is communication.

questions.prompt: What is a good way to find examples?

options.text: Copy examples that you find on a website
List things you are proud of and match each to a Behaviour
Pick a Behaviour and invent a story that fits it
Ask a friend to write them in your own words

questions.hint: Starting from your own experience is easier and more honest.

questions.prompt: How many things might you list to start?

options.text: None, as you do it on the day
One
Exactly twenty
Six to eight

questions.hint: A short list of six to eight gives enough choice.

questions.prompt: How recent should examples be?

options.text: Only from your time at school or college
Recent if possible, but older ones are fine if strong
Only from more than a year ago, never recent
Only from the last month, with nothing earlier

questions.hint: Strength matters more than date, though recent is helpful.

questions.prompt: Which of these can count as an educational example?

options.text: A holiday photograph
A bus pass for a student
A receipt from a shop
A group assignment

questions.hint: Group assignments involve teamwork and communication.

questions.prompt: What must be true of every example you use?

options.text: It took place in a paid role at an employer
It lasted for at least one year in total
It is true and you can answer follow-up questions
It involved a manager who can give a reference

questions.hint: Truth and the ability to explain it are essential.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of describing what you did?

options.text: To name the colleagues who worked with you
To list every job title you have held
To fill the space available on the form
To show the Behaviour in action

questions.hint: The assessor wants to see the Behaviour in what you did.

items.title: Level 2: What each part of STAR is for
items.body: Each part of STAR has a clear job. The Situation gives the assessor just enough background to understand your story. It answers questions such as where and when it happened and what was going on. Keep it to a sentence or two. The Task explains your own responsibility. It says what you were asked to do or what you decided had to be done. This stops the assessor assuming that someone else was in charge. The Action is the main part. It is where you describe, in order, what you personally did. Use the word I, and give steps rather than a general summary. For example, say 'I wrote down the questions, rang three suppliers and compared the quotes' instead of 'I looked into prices'. The Result completes the story by showing what happened because of what you did, and what you learned. A good Result is clear, and where possible has a number, such as a time saved or a sum raised. If the result was mixed, say so honestly and explain what you would do differently. A common mistake is to spend too long on the Situation and too little on the Action. A useful target is to keep the Situation and Task together to about a quarter of the answer, with the Action taking about half. The rest goes to the Result.

questions.prompt: What is the Situation in STAR meant to do?

options.text: To describe your main steps in order
To give just enough background
To state the outcome of what you did
To list all the people involved in it

questions.hint: The Situation is a brief setting of the scene.

questions.prompt: What does the Task in STAR show the assessor?

options.text: The qualifications you held at the time
Your own responsibility or aim
The time of year when it took place
The final result and what you learned

questions.hint: The Task says what you were asked or decided to do.

questions.prompt: Why does the Task matter?

options.text: It shows what you were responsible for
It hides how much others did for you
It makes the answer run to the word limit
It can replace the Action if space is short

questions.hint: It shows what you were responsible for.

questions.prompt: Which is the main part of a STAR answer?

options.text: The Action
The Task
The closing line
The Situation

questions.hint: The Action carries the most weight.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a better Action?

options.text: It was all dealt with in good time by the end of the week
I looked into the prices for the event and did my best
I wrote down the questions, rang three suppliers and compared quotes
We sorted the whole thing out between the group of us

questions.hint: It gives steps the assessor can picture.

questions.prompt: What does the Result show?

options.text: What happened because of what you did, and what you learned
Where the event took place and who attended
Who the other people involved in it were
What your job title was at the time of the event

questions.hint: The Result shows the effect and the learning.

questions.prompt: What makes a Result stronger?

options.text: A comment on what a friend thought of it
A list of all the skills you believe you have
A clear number, such as a time saved or a sum raised
A long description of the room where it took place

questions.hint: Numbers make the effect specific.

questions.prompt: What should you do if the result was mixed?

options.text: Leave out the parts that did not go as planned
Leave out the Result and finish after the Action
Describe it as a complete success in every way
Say so honestly and explain what you would do differently

questions.hint: Honest reflection shows learning.

questions.prompt: What is a common mistake in STAR answers?

options.text: Finishing the answer with a clear Result
Spending too long on the Situation and too little on the Action
Using the word I to describe what you did
Giving a number to show the size of the result

questions.hint: Too much background leaves little room for what you did.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much of an answer should the Action take?

options.text: About a quarter
About a tenth
About half
Almost none

questions.hint: A guide is to give the Action about half of the answer.

items.title: Level 2: Writing the Action and Result well
items.body: The difference between a weak and a strong STAR answer is often in the verbs. Weak answers use general phrases such as 'helped', 'dealt with' or 'got involved'. Strong answers use specific verbs that show what you did, such as 'I phoned', 'I wrote', 'I checked', 'I counted' and 'I explained'. They also put the steps in order so that the assessor can follow the story. Another sign of strength is detail that shows effort and choice. Why did you choose that method? Who did you ask for help? What did you do when something went wrong? Keep the language plain. You are not expected to use special words. Short sentences are easier to read and easier to mark. For the Result, say what changed for other people or for the work, for example 'the queue was cleared by 4 pm' or 'we received four new volunteers'. Then add what you learned, for example that you would check the numbers earlier next time. If an application form has a word limit, such as a few hundred words, plan the answer to fit before you write it. An answer that is cut off in the middle of the Result loses marks. Read your answer out loud to check it makes sense, and make sure that every sentence helps to show the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which verb phrase makes the strongest Action?

options.text: I was part of the group doing the rota
I got involved with the rota in the end
I helped out with the rota when I could
I phoned the school and arranged the rota

questions.hint: Specific verbs show what you actually did.

questions.prompt: Why are phrases like 'dealt with' weak?

options.text: They are too formal for an application form
They can sound rude to someone reading them
They are too long and take up the word limit
They do not say what you actually did

questions.hint: They are general and give the assessor nothing to score.

questions.prompt: Why should the steps be in order?

options.text: So that the answer comes out a little longer
So that you need fewer words to tell it
So the assessor can follow the story
So that the figures in it add up correctly

questions.hint: A clear sequence is easier to follow and mark.

questions.prompt: What kind of detail makes an answer stronger?

options.text: A list of all of the other jobs you have done
Why you chose a method and what you did when something went wrong
The colour and size of the building where it happened
Your full home address and the date you were born

questions.hint: Reasons and problem-solving show effort and choice.

questions.prompt: How should the language be?

options.text: Vague, with general terms
Technical, with long sentences
Plain, with short sentences
Formal, with legal words

questions.hint: Plain short sentences are easier to read and mark.

questions.prompt: Which Result is strongest?

options.text: It all went very well in the end
Everyone seemed to be happy afterwards
It turned out to be fine on the day
The queue was cleared by 4 pm

questions.hint: It states a specific effect.

questions.prompt: What should you add after saying what changed?

options.text: What you were paid
Who else was there
What you learned
Your age

questions.hint: Learning shows reflection.

questions.prompt: What happens if an answer is cut off at the word limit?

options.text: You are given a second chance to finish it
You may lose marks for a missing Result
The whole form is rejected by the system
The assessor adds the missing part for you

questions.hint: An unfinished Result leaves the story incomplete.

questions.prompt: When should you plan the answer to fit the word limit?

options.text: Only if the assessor asks you to
After you have submitted the form
On the day of the interview itself
Before you start writing it

questions.hint: Planning first avoids being cut off.

questions.prompt: What is a good check before you submit?

options.text: Read your answer aloud to see if it makes sense
Count how many commas you have used in it
Remove all of the numbers to keep it short
Ask a friend to rewrite it for you in full

questions.hint: Reading aloud shows gaps and awkward sentences.

items.title: Level 2: Turning home tasks into work skills
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Many people do not realise how much skill they use at home. The trick is to look at the task and ask what skill it needs. Looking after a child or an older relative involves planning appointments, keeping track of medicines, speaking to doctors and schools, and staying calm under pressure. These link to organising, communicating and handling stress. Managing a household budget involves working out what comes in and goes out, paying bills on time, comparing prices and keeping records. That links to handling money and keeping accurate records. Organising a family event, such as a wedding or a religious festival, involves making a plan, booking suppliers, keeping to a budget and working with other people. That links to planning, negotiating and teamwork. Helping a neighbour or family member with letters or forms involves reading carefully, explaining things simply and being patient. That links to communication. Volunteering at a food bank, a school or a place of worship adds working with the public and following rules. When you write about these tasks, use work language: 'I coordinated', 'I managed', 'I arranged' and 'I explained'. State numbers where you can, such as how many people, how much money or how often. Avoid words that play down what you did, such as 'just' or 'only'.

questions.prompt: Which skills does caring for an older relative involve?

options.text: Planning appointments and speaking to doctors
Operating heavy machinery in a workshop
Writing software for a computer system
Selling goods to customers in a shop

questions.hint: Caring involves organising, communicating and staying calm.

questions.prompt: Managing a household budget builds which skill?

options.text: Teaching a class of adult learners
Driving a delivery lorry on long journeys
Handling money and keeping records
Speaking in public to large audiences

questions.hint: Budgeting means tracking money and paying bills.

questions.prompt: Organising a family event builds which skill?

options.text: Typing documents at high speed
Planning and working with others
Filing company tax returns each year
Writing code for a small website

questions.hint: Events need plans, bookings, budgets and teamwork.

questions.prompt: Helping a neighbour with a form mainly builds which skill?

options.text: Cleaning
Communication
Technical qualification
Ability testing

questions.hint: Explaining things simply and patiently is communication.

questions.prompt: What does volunteering at a food bank add?

options.text: A regular wage paid every month
Working with the public and following rules
A recognised professional qualification
A university degree in a related subject

questions.hint: Volunteering gives experience of the public and of procedures.

questions.prompt: Which phrase uses work language?

options.text: I did whatever I was told to do on it
I just helped out with the rota a bit
I coordinated the rota for six volunteers
I only did the small jobs on the rota

questions.hint: It names an action and a number in work terms.

questions.prompt: Which words should you avoid?

options.text: Coordinated and explained
Just and only
Managed and arranged
Planned and booked

questions.hint: Words like just and only play down what you did.

questions.prompt: What helps an example from home life sound strong?

options.text: Numbers such as people, money or how often
A longer introduction before the story begins
An apology that it was done at home
A promise that you will try your best

questions.hint: Numbers make an example specific.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in spotting a home skill?

options.text: Ask whether you were paid for doing it
Look at the task and ask what skill it needs
Ask whether it was difficult to complete
Ask whether anybody saw you doing it

questions.hint: Linking tasks to skills reveals evidence.

questions.prompt: Keeping track of medicines for a relative shows which skill?

options.text: Advertising a service
Designing a product
Selling to customers
Accuracy and organisation

questions.hint: It requires careful records and routine.
